Richard Sibbes
RICH-erd SIBZ
proper noun (figure)
Germanic Richard — "strong ruler, hard-ruler." Surname Sibbes (also spelled Sibs, Sybbes, Sibbs in his lifetime), of uncertain English origin; possibly from sib ("kin, peace, peaceable"), an Old English personal name carried into surnames.

See also: Richard Sibbes

📖 Biblical Definition

Richard Sibbes (1577 — July 5, 1635 AD) was the great early-Stuart Puritan pastor and Cambridge-shaped "sweet dropper" whose The Bruised Reed and Smoking Flax (1630) became one of the most widely loved devotional works of the entire Puritan era and (according to Charles Spurgeon) the book that converted Richard Baxter. Born to a peasant-wheelwright's family in Tostock, Suffolk; educated at St. John's College, Cambridge (Master of Arts 1606); Fellow of St. John's; Lecturer at Holy Trinity, Cambridge (the great Puritan Cambridge preaching post) from 1610; Master of Catherine Hall (now St. Catharine's College), Cambridge from 1626; Preacher at Gray's Inn, London (one of the four Inns of Court) from 1617. His preaching at these three institutions made him the most influential preacher to the rising Puritan generation that would become the Westminster Assembly: John Cotton (later of New England), Thomas Goodwin, Thomas Manton, and (indirectly) Richard Baxter all named Sibbes as a decisive shaping influence. His gentle, Christological, pastorally-warm preaching earned him the nickname "the heavenly Doctor Sibbes" and "the sweet dropper" (the dripping-honey preacher). His Christology is among the most affectionate and union-with-Christ-saturated of the entire Puritan era. The Bruised Reed takes Matthew 12:20 ("A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory") as its text and over twenty meditations builds a pastoral theology of how Christ deals tenderly with weak and struggling believers. The book has never been out of print since 1630; the Banner of Truth Trust's modern reprint introduced a new generation of Reformed readers to the most pastorally tender of the early Stuart Puritans.

RICHARD SIBBES, proper noun. Germanic Richard ("strong ruler") + English surname (also Sibs, Sybbes; possibly from Old English sib, "peace, kin").

Early-Stuart English Puritan pastor (1577-1635 AD); Cambridge fellow, Master of Catherine Hall (now St. Catharine's College) from 1626; Preacher at Gray's Inn, London from 1617.

Author of The Bruised Reed and Smoking Flax (1630), The Soul's Conflict (1635), and many sermons. Called 'the heavenly Doctor Sibbes' and 'the sweet dropper'.

Decisive shaping influence on John Cotton, Thomas Goodwin, Thomas Manton; The Bruised Reed was credited by Spurgeon as the book that converted Richard Baxter.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 12:20 — "A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory."

Isaiah 42:1-3 — "Behold my servant, whom I uphold; mine elect, in whom my soul delighteth... A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth."

2 Corinthians 12:9 — "And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."

Hebrews 4:15-16 — "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Richard Sibbes is corrupted when his pastoral gentleness is misread as theological softness (he was a thoroughly Reformed-confessional theologian whose tender pulpit served a robust doctrine), when his union-with-Christ emphasis is dismissed as mere mysticism, or when his decisive influence on the next-generation Puritans is overlooked because his own published works are slimmer than theirs.

expand to see more

Gentleness-as-softness misreading. Sibbes's nickname 'the sweet dropper' and the tender pastoral tone of The Bruised Reed have sometimes been read as evidence that he was less rigorously Reformed than later Puritans like Owen. The historical record is otherwise: Sibbes was Lecturer at Holy Trinity, Cambridge (the great Puritan post), Master of Catherine Hall, Preacher at Gray's Inn, and held confessional Reformed positions on every contested point of his era (eternal decree, total depravity, particular atonement, perseverance of the saints, sacramental theology). His gentleness was pastoral, not doctrinal. The bruised-reed compassion served a Reformed doctrine that taught Christ's tenderness as the gospel-shape of Reformed pastoral care.

Union-with-Christ as mysticism. Sibbes's preaching is unusually saturated with the language of Christ's love for the soul, marriage-union imagery from Song of Solomon, and the believer's affective communion with the risen Lord. Some twentieth-century Reformed readers, formed by Princeton-style scholastic theology, treat this affective register as quasi-mystical and not fully Reformed. The historical record shows that this affective union-with-Christ register was a recognized strand of Reformed orthodoxy from Calvin through the Westminster Divines — Calvin himself spent considerable space in the Institutes on union with Christ. Read Sibbes affectively; do not relegate him to mysticism.
